## What will we learn?

Can clinical measurements help us distinguish patients with and without heart
disease? We will first read the results of a random forest already fitted to
these data. Then we will build a neural network and examine its predictions.

By the end, you should be able to explain a model's mistakes, fit a neural
network with Keras, and use `mlr3` to evaluate its predictions.

Have the [session guide](guide.qmd) ready before starting. It covers opening the
project and installing Keras. The code below assumes your working folder is
`part2/`. Run the code blocks in order in RStudio during the session. Saved results let
us discuss the examples before fitting our own network.

## 1. Meet the heart data

Each row describes one patient. There are 270 patients and 13 measurements,
including age, chest pain and cholesterol. The outcome, `heart_disease`, tells
us whether heart disease is `absent` or `present`. We are classifying existing
heart disease, rather than estimating future risk.

Load the prepared data. The data script gives the categories readable labels.

```{r}
#| label: neural-data
# Load the patient measurements and outcome labels.
source("R/01-data.R")
```

Count the patients in each outcome group:

```{r}
table(heart$heart_disease)
```

There are 150 patients without heart disease and 120 with heart disease.
A **predictor** is a measurement we use to help predict the outcome. The outcome
itself must not be included among the predictors.

**Discuss:** Which measurements might help distinguish the two groups?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Discussion: possible predictors"}
Chest-pain type, exercise-induced angina, maximum heart rate and exercise ECG
measurements are plausible candidates. The vessel count and thal test result
may also help distinguish the groups. Age, blood pressure and cholesterol may
contribute alongside these measurements. These are starting hypotheses, not a
computed ranking of importance. We need data and evaluation to establish which
patterns help prediction in this sample. Predictive usefulness does not establish
that a measurement causes disease.
:::

For a visual explanation of single trees, see the optional
[Trees and pruning companion](trees-and-pruning.qmd). It explains Figures 1–3
and why pruning can leave a tree looking similar to the default tree.

## 2. Read the random forest results

A random forest combines predictions from many decision trees. We have already
fitted this model using 180 patients and tested it on the other 90. The test
patients were kept out of training so we could assess predictions on unseen
observations. We will use the saved results here, without fitting the forest
again.

### What did the model get right and wrong?

A **confusion matrix** counts correct predictions and mistakes. Read the rows
as the model's predictions and the columns as the patients' recorded outcomes.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Read the saved confusion matrix"
forest_confusion <- read.csv("outputs/confusion.csv")
forest_table <- xtabs(Freq ~ response + truth, data = forest_confusion)
knitr::kable(forest_table, caption = "Random forest: predictions for 90 test patients")
```

The model correctly identified 30 patients with heart disease and 45 without it.
It missed 7 patients who had heart disease (**false negatives**) and raised
8 false alarms in patients without heart disease (**false positives**).

**Discuss:** What might a missed case mean for a patient? What might a false
alarm lead to?

### How well did it perform?

**Accuracy** is the proportion of all test patients classified correctly.
**Sensitivity** is the proportion of patients with heart disease correctly
identified. **Specificity** is the proportion without heart disease correctly
identified.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Read the saved forest scores"
forest_scores <- read.csv("outputs/holdout-measures.csv")
measure_ids <- c("classif.acc", "classif.tpr", "classif.tnr")
measure_labels <- c("Accuracy", "Sensitivity", "Specificity")
forest_values <- forest_scores$value[match(measure_ids, forest_scores$measure)]

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Measure = measure_labels, Percent = round(100 * forest_values, 1)),
  caption = "Saved random forest results (%)"
)
```

Accuracy is 83.3%: 75 correct predictions out of 90. Sensitivity is 81.1% and
specificity is 84.9%. Looking at all three helps us see what accuracy alone
can hide.

The forest predicts probabilities. A **threshold** is the probability at which
we decide to classify a patient as having heart disease. Lowering the threshold
usually catches more cases, but also raises more false alarms.

![The ROC curve shows sensitivity against the false-positive rate as the probability threshold changes. The diagonal represents chance-level discrimination.](figures/04-roc.png){fig-align="center"}

**Discuss:** Would you choose a threshold using accuracy alone?

### How to read the evaluation curves

The **ROC curve (Figure 4)** compares sensitivity with the false-positive rate
(`1 − specificity`) as the probability threshold changes. The saved curve sits
above the diagonal: it shows useful discrimination on these test patients.
The upper-left corner represents high sensitivity with few false alarms.
The curve does not identify a clinically appropriate cut-off on its own.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Figure 4 extensions: precision–recall and thresholds"}
The optional script also saves two other views of the same forest predictions.
**Recall** is sensitivity, and **precision** is positive predictive value: the
share of positive predictions that are correct. Their curve shows the balance
as the threshold changes; precision also depends on disease frequency.

The threshold plot shows **classification error**, the fraction of incorrect
predictions, for different cut-offs. A lower point means fewer total mistakes
on these test patients. It does not give separate sensitivity/specificity curves
or establish an optimal clinical threshold. Missed cases and false alarms can
have different consequences. Choose a threshold using training/validation data
and a stated purpose, then assess it on separate evaluation data.

![Saved forest precision–recall curve for the 90 test patients.](figures/04-prc.png){fig-align="center"}

![Saved forest classification error across probability thresholds.](figures/04-threshold.png){fig-align="center"}
:::

### Why move to a neural network?

The forest provides a baseline. A neural network gives us a different way to
learn from the same measurements: trees divide patients into groups, whereas
a network learns weighted combinations of inputs. We explore whether that
change affects accuracy and the types of mistake. We keep the test patients
consistent; adding complexity does not guarantee better predictions.

## 3. Use mlr3 to organise the prediction task

We now ask the same question using a neural network. We keep the same training
and test patients so the results can be compared.

`mlr3` helps organise a prediction problem. A **task** records the data and the
outcome we want to predict. Here, `present` is the **positive class**: the
condition we want to detect. We load the saved split instead of drawing a new
one.

```{r}
#| label: neural-task
library(mlr3)
# Tell mlr3 which outcome to predict and which class means disease is present.
heart_task <- as_task_classif(heart,
  target = "heart_disease",
  positive = "present",
  id = "heart"
)
# Reuse the patients used to train and test the saved random forest.
split_record <- read.csv("outputs/split.csv")
split <- list(
  train = split_record$row_id[split_record$subset == "train"],
  test = split_record$row_id[split_record$subset == "test"]
)
```

The training group contains 180 patients; the test group contains 90. Keep the
test patients aside until the network has finished learning.

### Why separate a task from a learner?

A **task** defines the prediction problem: the dataset, outcome and positive
class. A **learner** defines the method used to learn predictions. In script 2,
`lrn("classif.ranger", predict_type = "prob")` creates a random-forest learner;
`train()` fits it on the training rows and `predict()` evaluates other rows.
The task itself does not create the split.

In script 3, we define the task again and reuse the saved row numbers, but
**Keras builds and trains the neural network directly**. We do not create an
mlr3 neural-network learner here. Later, `PredictionClassif` lets mlr3 evaluate
Keras predictions with the same measures as the forest.

If you explored the tree plots first, the transition is from understanding
fitted structure to evaluating predictions. The forest is a new model combining
many trees; it does not reuse the single `rpart` tree we plotted.

## 4. Prepare the inputs

Keras needs numerical inputs. We turn categories into numbers and indicator
columns. An **indicator** is a column containing 0 or 1 to show whether a category
applies. This gives us 22 input columns from the original 13 predictors.

We also **scale** numerical measurements so differences in units, such as age
and cholesterol, do not dominate the learning process. Scaling is learned from
the fitting rows only, keeping validation and test patients out of that step.

```{r}
#| label: neural-inputs
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show input preparation"
# Exclude the outcome from the inputs. Keras needs numbers, so use 0/1 for
# binary categories and indicator columns for the others. An indicator is 1
# when a category applies and 0 otherwise. Together these give 22 inputs.
x_data <- heart[, setdiff(names(heart), "heart_disease")]
for (nm in c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")) {
  x_data[[nm]] <- as.integer(x_data[[nm]]) - 1L
}
nominal <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.factor, logical(1))]
contrasts_full <- lapply(x_data[nominal], function(x) contrasts(x, contrasts = FALSE))
x <- model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = x_data, contrasts.arg = contrasts_full)
stopifnot(ncol(x) == 22L, all(is.finite(x)))
# Keras reserves the last 20% of training rows for validation.
# Calculate scaling from the other 80% only, keeping validation and test
# patients out of this calculation.
inner_n <- floor(length(split$train) * 0.8)
fit_rows <- split$train[seq_len(inner_n)]
continuous <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.numeric, logical(1))]
continuous <- setdiff(
  continuous,
  c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")
)
# Subtract each measurement's mean and divide by its standard deviation.
# This puts measurements with different units on a comparable scale.
centre <- colMeans(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE])
spread <- apply(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
stopifnot(all(spread > 0))
x[, continuous] <- sweep(
  sweep(x[, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, centre),
  2, spread, "/"
)
# Code the outcome as 1 for present and 0 for absent.
y <- as.integer(heart$heart_disease == "present")
```

Check the number of input columns and the outcome coding:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ncol(x)
table(y)
```

The outcome is coded as 1 for heart disease and 0 for its absence.

### Why are there 22 inputs?

`model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = x_data, contrasts.arg = contrasts_full)` creates
one numerical row per patient. In the formula, `.` includes all predictors and
`- 1` removes the intercept column. `contrasts_full` requests an indicator for
every level of each remaining categorical predictor.

| Original predictors | Columns in `x` |
| --- | ---: |
| Six numerical measurements/counts | 6 |
| Three binary predictors, already converted to 0/1 | 3 |
| Chest-pain type (4), resting ECG (3), ST slope (3), thal (3) | 13 |
| **Total** | **22** |

For example, a patient with typical angina has 1 in that chest-pain indicator
column and 0 in the other three. The result is a **270 × 22 matrix**. The outcome
is excluded from `x` and stored separately in `y`.

### What do centre, spread and sweep do?

`centre` stores each selected column's mean among the **144 fitting patients**.
`spread` stores its standard deviation, a measure of variation. We standardise
each continuous column using:

```text
centred value = original value − fitting mean
scaled value = centred value / fitting standard deviation
```

The inner `sweep()` subtracts `centre`; subtraction is its default operation.
The outer `sweep()` divides by `spread` using `"/"`. The argument `2` means
operate column by column. `drop = FALSE` keeps the selection as a matrix even
if only one column is selected. The assignment writes the scaled values back
into the continuous columns of `x`, leaving binary and indicator columns unchanged.

For a conceptual example, a fitting mean age of 55 and standard deviation of
10 would transform age 65 into `(65 − 55) / 10 = 1`. These example values are
illustrative, not summaries calculated from our data.

We apply the **same fitting means and standard deviations** to validation and
test patients. This puts measurements with different units on comparable scales
without using those patients to estimate the scaling. Once `x` and `y` are ready,
we can define the network.

## 5. Build the network with Keras

Keras defines and trains the neural network. We use it directly here, then bring
its predictions into `mlr3` for evaluation.

Think of the network as a sequence:

**Patient measurements → hidden layers → probability of heart disease**

A **hidden layer** combines inputs into patterns that the network learns.
The final layer returns one probability between 0 and 1. The two hidden layers
below contain 64 and 32 units. **Dropout** temporarily switches off some units
during training to help limit overfitting: learning the training examples too
closely to work well on new patients.

```{r}
#| label: neural-build
#| eval: false
library(keras3)
# Fix the random starting point for the network.
set_random_seed(20261023)

# Pass 22 inputs through two hidden layers to one output probability.
# Dropout temporarily switches off some units during training to limit overfitting.
network <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(22)) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 32, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
# Choose how to update the weights and measure prediction error.
# Binary cross-entropy is a loss for a two-class outcome.
compile(network,
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.002),
  loss = "binary_crossentropy", metrics = "accuracy"
)
```

`compile()` sets how the network learns. The **optimiser** updates its weights
(the values controlling its connections). The **loss** measures prediction error;
binary cross-entropy is used for this two-class outcome.

### What does each layer do?

`keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(22))` defines a model whose layers connect
in order. Each patient supplies 22 numbers; 22 is the number of input columns,
not the number of patients. A container created with only this input shape can
show no layers and zero parameters. The dense layers add the trainable weights.

| Component | Role in this network |
| --- | --- |
| Dense, 64 units, ReLU | Each unit combines all 22 inputs using learned weights and a bias. ReLU keeps positive signals and returns zero for negative ones, allowing nonlinear patterns. |
| Dropout, rate 0.4 | Randomly sets 40% of the preceding layer's outputs to zero at each training step to help limit overfitting. |
| Dense, 32 units, ReLU | Learns further combinations of the signals from the preceding layer. |
| Dropout, rate 0.4 | Also regularises the second hidden layer. |
| Dense, 1 unit, sigmoid | Converts the final signal into a value between 0 and 1, interpreted as an estimated probability of disease present. |

**Dense** means every unit connects to every output of the preceding layer.
Dropout operates during training and switches off for prediction. The 64/32
units and 0.4 dropout follow the reference architecture; they are settings we
could investigate through tuning, rather than proven optimal choices.
The complete architecture has 3,585 trainable parameters, including biases.

The architecture defines the calculation. `compile()` selects the learning rules:
Adam updates the weights, and binary cross-entropy measures probability prediction
error. **`fit()` is the step that learns the weights from patients.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="If creating the model takes time"}
The first Keras call in a fresh R session may also initialise Python and the
backend. Creating the model container does not train the network. A persistent
wait or an error warrants checking the Keras setup in the [session guide](guide.qmd);
it is not evidence that 22 inputs are too many.
:::

## 6. Fit the network and watch it learn

An **epoch** is one pass through the fitting data. A **batch** is a smaller group
processed before updating the weights.

We reserve 20% of the training group for **validation**: checking progress during
learning. The network updates its weights using 144 patients and monitors its
progress on 36 validation patients. These are separate from the 90 test patients.
Early stopping ends training if validation loss stops improving.

```{r}
#| label: neural-fit
#| eval: false
# An epoch is one pass through the fitting rows; batches contain 32 rows.
# Monitor validation loss and stop after 10 epochs without improvement,
# restoring the weights from the best validation epoch.
training <- fit(
  network,
  x[split$train, ],
  y[split$train],
  epochs = 50,
  batch_size = 32,
  validation_split = 0.2,
  verbose = 1,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(patience = 10, restore_best_weights = TRUE))
)
```

Plot the history from your own run:

```{r}
#| label: neural-history
#| eval: false
# Compare training and validation loss as learning progresses.
plot(training)
```

Look for training and validation loss in this plot. The figure below comes
from the saved workshop run; your run may produce a different curve.

![Saved neural-network run: training and validation loss across successive passes through the fitting data. Lower loss means smaller prediction error.](figures/05-neural-loss.png){fig-align="center"}

If training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises, the network may be
overfitting.

**Discuss:** Why do we need validation patients as well as training patients?

### Why keep fitting, validation and test patients separate?

| Group | Patients | What we use them for |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Fitting | 144 | Update the network weights using prediction errors. |
| Validation | 36 | Monitor learning and select the stopping epoch, without updating weights from these rows. |
| Test | 90 | Assess predictions after fitting and model choices are complete. |

Training error alone can fall because the network learns details of its examples.
Validation asks whether those improvements also help patients outside the weight
updates. Because validation influences the stopping decision, it cannot replace
the final test group. Early stopping uses patience 10: after ten epochs without
improvement in validation loss, training ends and restores the best weights.

### How to read Figure 5

The blue curve is fitting/training loss and the red curve is validation loss.
Both initially fall, suggesting that learning also helps the validation patients.
Later, training loss continues downward, while validation loss levels off and
rises slightly. More training is then improving the fit without improving
validation performance, a warning of overfitting.

The saved history contains 27 epochs; its lowest validation loss occurs at
epoch 17. This agrees with stopping after ten further epochs without improvement.
These are the saved run's curves, not a guarantee for a new run.

This connects to tree pruning: both pruning and early stopping help control
complexity, through different mechanisms. Neither proves performance on new
patients; the separate test group supplies the final evaluation.

## 7. Evaluate the network and compare results

Use the trained network to predict probabilities for the 90 test patients.
For this example, classify a probability of 0.5 or more as `present`.

`PredictionClassif$new()` puts the Keras predictions into an `mlr3` prediction
object. It stores the observed outcomes, predicted classes and probabilities.
We can then request the same measures used for the forest.

```{r}
#| label: neural-predict
#| eval: false
# Predict unseen test patients. Use 0.5 as the cut-off for a present prediction.
prob <- as.numeric(predict(network, x[split$test, ], verbose = 0))
class <- ifelse(prob >= 0.5, "present", "absent")
accuracy <- mean(class == as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
accuracy

# Bring the Keras predictions into mlr3 for the same evaluation measures.
network_pred <- PredictionClassif$new(
  task = heart_task,
  row_ids = split$test,
  truth = heart_task$truth(rows = split$test),
  response = class,
  prob = cbind(present = prob, absent = 1 - prob)
)
network_pred$confusion
network_pred$score(msrs(c("classif.acc", "classif.tpr", "classif.tnr")))
```

### What happened in the saved run?

The next table uses the saved network predictions, rather than fitting a new
network when the page opens.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Compare the saved results"
saved_network <- read.csv("outputs/neural-predictions.csv")
stopifnot(
  identical(saved_network$row_id, split$test),
  identical(saved_network$truth, as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
)
saved_prediction <- PredictionClassif$new(
  task = heart_task,
  row_ids = saved_network$row_id,
  truth = heart_task$truth(rows = saved_network$row_id),
  response = saved_network$prediction,
  prob = cbind(
    present = saved_network$probability_present,
    absent = 1 - saved_network$probability_present
  )
)
network_values <- unname(saved_prediction$score(msrs(measure_ids)))
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Measure = measure_labels,
    `Random forest (%)` = round(100 * forest_values, 1),
    `Neural network (%)` = round(100 * network_values, 1),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Saved results for the same 90 test patients"
)
```

The saved network classified 77 of the 90 test patients correctly, compared
with 75 for the forest. That small difference in one split does not establish
that neural networks are generally better. Compare the types of mistakes as
well as the overall accuracy. After your own run, use `network_pred` above to
inspect your results; this saved comparison table remains a reference.

**Discuss:** Which model missed fewer cases? Is the difference large enough to
change your conclusion?

### What improved, and what did not?

| Saved test result | Random forest | Keras network |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Correct predictions | 75/90 | 77/90 |
| Missed disease cases | 7 | 8 |
| False alarms | 8 | 5 |

Network accuracy increased by **2.2 percentage points** after rounding. It made
three fewer false alarms but missed one more disease case. Whether that balance
is preferable depends on the purpose and consequences of the prediction.

We evaluated the **random forest and Keras network** here. The single-tree plots
illustrate fitting and pruning; they do not provide a third held-out score.
Both evaluated models use the same 90 test patients, but the forest fits on all
180 training patients and the network uses 144 for fitting plus 36 for validation.
The models also use different input representations. These saved local runs
support a teaching comparison, not a controlled demonstration that one method
is generally superior.

A prediction estimates the recorded outcome from measurements. It does not
identify what caused the patient's disease, and this example does not forecast
future cardiovascular risk.

## What have we learned about machine learning?

**Machine learning uses examples to learn a rule for making predictions.** We
choose the outcome, available inputs, model structure and learning procedure;
the algorithm uses fitting data to determine its internal rules or values.
A tree learns splits, a forest combines many trees, and a neural network learns
connection weights.

The full workflow is to prepare inputs, fit the model, monitor validation and
assess predictions on patients outside fitting. A lower training error alone
is insufficient. We consider accuracy alongside the kinds of mistake, and keep
our conclusions within the limits of one small dataset and one test split.

The main session can end here. Resampling would next ask how stable the results
are when the patients used for fitting and evaluation change.

These scripts run separately. The tree/evaluation script also refits the random
forest; it is not needed for the main session.

### Resampling: how stable are the results?

Cross-validation rotates which group stays out of fitting. Repeated subsampling
uses different splits; bootstrap samples fitting rows with replacement. Script 2
includes three-fold cross-validation, 100 subsampling repetitions and 40 bootstrap
repetitions for a **100-tree forest**, evaluating AUC. Those scores use a different
measure and evaluation design from the main holdout accuracy comparison.

For a new model comparison, use the same folds and measures for both methods.
Estimate preprocessing inside each fitting fold and keep model/threshold selection
separate from evaluation. Repeatedly changing a model to improve the test results
we have already examined would weaken that test set's independence.

### Tuning: can different settings help?

[Script 4](R/04-tuning.R) tunes an **XGBoost model**, a boosted-tree method; it does
not tune the Keras network or the main random forest. It searches over the number
and depth of trees, learning rate and regularisation strength. Grid search tries
a fixed collection of settings, random search samples settings, and model-based
optimisation uses earlier trials to guide the next ones. Ten-fold cross-validation
within the training group compares candidate settings.

Nested cross-validation separates selection from evaluation: inner folds choose
settings and outer folds assess the whole selection process. The saved validation
record reports completed 500-configuration random search and 30-configuration
model-based search. The full grid and full-budget nested workflow have only had
reduced smoke tests; they are not completed full runs. Tuning does not guarantee
an improvement. See the [validation record](outputs/validation.qmd) before running
these potentially long extensions.

### Synthetic data: what do artificial records represent?

[Script 5](R/05-synthetic-data.R) uses an adversarial random forest to learn patterns
in the observed data. `forde()` estimates a distribution from the fitted forest,
and `forge()` samples 270 artificial records from it. The generated table is saved
separately as `outputs/synthetic-heart.csv`.

Compare age summaries and outcome proportions with the real data as an initial
check, then consider relationships between variables and the intended use.
Synthetic records are examples for exploration and teaching, not additional
observed patients or independent evidence of predictive performance. Generating
them does not automatically guarantee privacy.
